en: The Jātaka,
Great Collection, Chapter on the Mūgapakkha (The Dumb and Paralysed)
6. The Bhūridatta Jātaka:
“Whatever jewels there are in the abode of Dhatarattha;”
“May all these things be yours;
give your daughter to the king.
“We have no marriage alliance with the Nāgas.”
Never before has such a thing been done;
how can we perform this improper marriage?
“Surely you have abandoned your life,
or even your kingdom, O lord of men,
for when the Naga is enraged, [nothing remains].”
Such as these live long. You,
O King, being a human, are one who lacks supernatural power compared to one who possesses it.
"You slight the son of Varuṇa,
the Yāmuna. "I do not slight the king," [he replied].
The illustrious Dhatarattha;
for Dhatarattha is the lord even of many nāgas.
"Though he is of great power, that Kshatriya of the Videhas is not worthy of my daughter."
“Let the noble Samuddajā arise;
announce all the nāgas. “Let Kambala and Assatara arise;
announce all the nāgas.”
“Let them go forth at Benares, and let them not harm anyone.
“In dwellings, in pits, in... [the text continues]”
Let them hang from the streets and at the crossroads,
from the tops of trees and stretched across the archways.
I too shall surround this great and vast city with all-white treasures.
"Causing fear among the people of Kāsī.
Having heard those words of his,
the many-colored serpents—
They went forth in Bārāṇasī and did not harm anyone;
in their dwellings and in the caves, they lived in peace.
On the streets and in the squares,
they hung from the treetops and were spread across the archways.
Seeing them hanging there,
many women wailed aloud upon seeing the elephants with their trunks severed.
As he breathed in and out again and again,
Benares trembled and fell into a state of distress.
Raising her arms and crying out, she said,
"Give your daughter to the king!
"In the midst of the flower-offering forest,"
Who is this woman with blood-red eyes and broad shoulders?
Who are these ten well-dressed women, wearing bracelets and armlets, standing here paying homage?
Who are you, O long-armed one, shining so brightly in the midst of the forest like a fire sprinkled with ghee?
You are some powerful yakkha of great authority.
"Or are you a Nāga of great power?
"I am a Nāga possessed of supernormal powers,
radiant and difficult to overcome."
Enraged, I could consume even a prosperous kingdom with my splendor;
for Samuddajā was indeed my mother.
Dhataraṭṭha was my father;
I am the youngest, Sudassana,
known to the wise as Bhūridatta.
That deep, ever-whirling,
and fearsome lake which you behold—
this is my divine abode.
Many hundreds of men [were there].
From the midst of the forest came the blue water,
resounding with the cries of peacocks and cranes.
Enter the Yamunā without fear;
it is secure, well-situated, and auspicious.
Having reached it there with your followers, you shall dwell at ease.
Together with your son, O brahmin;
honored by me with sensual pleasures,
you shall go happily, O brahmin.
The earth is level on every side, abundant with tagara,
and covered with *indagopaka* insects.
It shines with the most excellent greenery.
Delightful are the forest shrines,
delightful with the warbling of swans.
Lotus flowers stand upon well-constructed lotus ponds;
the pillars are well-fashioned with eight facets.
All are made of beryl;
the palaces with their thousand pillars shine,
filled with maidens.
You have been reborn in a celestial mansion,
divine through your own merits—
unconfined, auspicious, and delightful.
"Endowed with ultimate happiness—
O Thousand-Eyed One, I think you do not even desire that celestial mansion."
"For this power of yours is vast,
like that of the radiant Sakka.
"It cannot even be reached by the mind," [he replied].
The majesty and splendor of those who exercise power,
including Indra and the Vasus, as they move about.
Coveting that celestial mansion,
while observing the Uposatha day, one who seeks the happiness of the immortals—
“...on top of a half-buried anthill.
“And I, seeking deer,
entered the forest together with my son;”
My kinsmen do not recognize me, whether as dead or as living.
I call out to Bhūridatta:
The illustrious son of Kāsi; permitted by you,
may we also see our kinsmen.”
“Indeed, that was my desire,
that you remain in my presence;
for such sensual pleasures as these do not exist.”
These things are easily obtained among humans.
If you desire a dwelling, you shall be honored by me with all my desires.
"I have given you my permission;
may you see your kinsmen in safety.
"I shall wear this divine jewel," [he said].
One finds cattle and sons;
being healthy and happy,
one should go along taking them with him, O Brahmin.
“I welcome your words, Bhūridatta; they are wholesome.
I shall go forth, for I am old.”
One should not long for sensual pleasures.
If there is a failure in the holy life,
it must be remedied by means of wealth.
“If you come without wavering,
I will give you much wealth.
“I acknowledge your kindness.”
"O Bhūridatta, I shall heed your word;
I will come again if there should be need."
Having said this, Bhūridatta dispatched four men:
“Come, go, arise! he said.
"Quickly bring forth the brahmin.
Having heard those words of his,
four men rose up.
Sent by Bhūridatta,
they quickly brought the brahmin there.
Having taken up the auspicious gem, they said:
"Whose is this jewel, so well-acquired, so pleasing to the mind, so beautiful in form,
and so perfect in its craftsmanship?"
“Surrounded on all sides by a thousand red-eyed women,
today I go upon the path to death.”
“I have obtained this jewel.
“This rock has been well-tended,
always honored and revered;”
Well-maintained and well-applied,
it succeeds in every respect;
but for one whose practice is impaired—
Whether for depositing or for retaining—
this rock leads to destruction when it is cultivated in an improper manner.
An unskilled person is not worthy to wear this divine jewel;
follow instead the path of the virtuous.
“This body is my jewel. “And this gem of mine is not to be bartered for cows or for jewels;”
“A gem complete in both its brilliance and its facets is not for sale from me.
“If that gem is not for sale by you,” [he said].
Whether by cattle or by jewels;
now, by what may this gem be sold?
Tell me that when I ask you.”
“To him who has praised me as a great naga,
radiant and difficult to overcome,
to him I would give this rock.”
“Like the ocean with its radiance.
“Who indeed, in the guise of a brahmin,
is the best of winged creatures as they fly?”
He sought a nāga,
desiring to seize it as food for himself.
"I am not the lord of birds," [he said].
"I have not seen the garuḍa;
I was bitten by a venomous snake—
know me, O Brahmin, as one who has been struck down."
“What power do you possess?
What craft is known to you?
Or in what are you so overconfident?”
Do you not revere the serpent? [He replied:
"The forest-dwelling seer, who has long practiced austerities..."
Supaṇṇa declared the unsurpassed science of poisons to Kosiya;
he was one whose self was fully developed.
Within the mountain range,
I attended upon him with care,
unwearied day and night.
Thus, at that time, he was one by whom I was well-served,
a speaker and a practitioner of the holy life;
he revealed the divine mantra.
The Blessed One is my desire.
Relying on those mantras,
I am confident and do not fear the serpents.
“The Teacher is the destroyer of poisons;
know me as Alampāna.
“We take the jewel, dear father.”
“O Somadatta, understand this:
do not seek to seize our glory by means of force;
we shall abandon it of our own accord.”
“O Brahmin, whoever honors one who has reached his own home—
such is the result for one who performs wholesome deeds.”
Why do you desire evil out of delusion?
If you desire wealth,
Bhūridatta will show it to you.
Go to him and ask;
he will give you much wealth.
“Whatever has come into his hands or onto his plate...”
It is better to eat what is scattered here;
let not our present welfare,
O Somadatta, be passed over.
“The betrayer of friends and the forsaker of the beneficial is cooked in a terrible hell, even if he opens wide the earth.”
Even Jīvaka himself will wither away.
If you desire wealth,
Bhūridatta will show it to you.
"I think you will experience the enmity you have wrought against yourself before long.
"Having performed a great sacrifice..."
In this way the brahmins are purified;
we shall perform a great sacrifice,
and in this way we shall be released from evil.
“Now, indeed, I shall depart;
I will not stay with you today.
I would not go even a single step further.”
"So it is for one who commits evil.
Having said this to his father,
the learned Somadatta—
Having terrified the beings,
he departed from that place,
saying, "Seize this great nāga!"
Bring me this gem,
which has the luster of an *indagopaka* insect and a red head.
This body appears like a heap of cotton seeds;
it lies there like the top of an anthill.
“Take that, O Brahmin. Then,
with divine herbs,
he performed the recitation and the mantra-words.
Thus he was able to protect himself by performing a safeguard for the Teacher:
"Seeing me approaching..."
For you who have all desires fulfilled,
your senses are unimpaired and your face is radiant with joy.
Just as a lotus held in the hand is crushed by the palm,
so too has your face become withered.
Having seen me in such a state, I wonder: do you not speak to me?
Are you free from pain?
“By which [reason] did that evil omen come to your face upon seeing me?
“I saw a dream, dear father.”
One month ago from now,
my right arm was severed and smeared with blood as if it were my own.
A man took me and departed while I was weeping;
from that time on, I have seen this dream.
O Sudassana, understand this:
consequently, neither by day nor by night,
do I find any happiness.”
“Those maidens of beautiful form who formerly surrounded me,
covered with nets of gold— ”
Bhūridatta is not to be seen—
he who was formerly surrounded by those bearing excellent nets.
The kaṇikāra trees are in full bloom,
yet Bhūridatta is not to be seen.
Come now, let us go.
In the residence of Bhūridatta,
we behold your brother, established in the Dhamma and perfected in virtue.
And seeing Bhūridatta’s mother approaching,
he raised his arms and cried out.
The women of Bhūridatta said:
"We do not know of a son born to you within the last month."
Whether dead or alive,
Bhūridatta of great renown— like a bird whose young have been slain,
I am consumed with grief.
Seeing the bird’s nest empty,
I shall meditate for a long time in sorrow,
not seeing Bhūridatta.
The female osprey, her bow broken,
seeing her nest empty,
will brood with long-lasting sorrow.
She does not see Bhūridatta.
She is surely like a female cakravāka bird in a pond that has no water.
I shall meditate long in suffering,
not seeing Bhūridatta,
like a lamp in a smithy.
"I meditate within, not without;
thus I meditate in sorrow,
not seeing Bhūridatta."
Shaken like a sal tree and crushed by a tempestuous wind,
children and wives lie prostrate.
In the residence of Bhūridatta.
Having heard this cry in the residence of Bhūridatta;
Ariṭṭha and Subhoga ran right after him.
"Mother, take heart; do not grieve."
For living beings are of such a nature:
they pass away and they are reborn;
this is their destiny.
“I too know this, dear father;
for living beings are of such a nature.
When one is overcome by sorrow, [they do not see the way].”
He does not see Bhūridatta.
O Sudassana, know this for certain today during this very night:
"Without seeing Bhūridatta, I think I shall lose my life.
"Mother, take heart; do not grieve."
We shall bring back our brother;
we will go in every direction,
wandering in search of our brother.
On mountains, in difficult mountain passes,
in villages, and in market towns;
within less than seven nights—
"Behold your brother who has come!
Like a snake released from its hand,
he falls heavily at your feet."
“Is it not a snake that bit you, dear one?
Do not fear; be at ease.
“This was no serpent for me,” he replied.
Enough for the suffering of some;
as far as there is grasping,
nothing exists that is greater than I.”
“Who is this who has come to the assembly,
intoxicated with the guise of a brahmin?
Let him challenge us to a fair fight!”
“Let the assembly hear me:
‘You have been embraced by a naga;
I have been embraced by a female frog.’”
"Let it not be a marvel there,
even with five thousand [men]. "For I,
Vasumā, am wealthy," he said.
"You are poor, young man;
who indeed can be your guarantor,
and what could be your deposit?"
If I were to have a wager and there were such a guarantor,
let there be a miracle for us in that regard.
“By five thousand [men].
“Listen to my words, O Great King; may it be well with you.”
"For five thousand,
Kittima, I am indeed a guarantor for you.
"Or it may be a debt inherited from my ancestors."
Or whatever else has been made by yourself—
why do you, O brahmin, ask me for so much wealth?
“Alampāna indeed wishes to overcome me with his elephant;
I [will overcome him] with the frog-charm.”
"I shall bite the brahmin.
You, O Great King, Ruler of the Realm, must see him today."
Surrounded by the assembly of khattiyas,
go forth to see the snake. "I do not hold you in contempt."
“O young man, because of your talk of craft,
you are excessively proud of your skill;
you do not show proper respect for the serpent.”
“I too do not despise you on account of your craft, O brahmin,
nor because of the non-venomous Nāga.”
You utterly deceive people.
If people knew this about you as I know it,
[they would not trust you].
“You do not obtain anything at all, you glutton;
how could you have a fistful of grain, let alone wealth?
“I am one with a rough antelope skin, matted hair, and a foul mouth.”
Likewise, you have come to this assembly;
you, being ignorant, treat this Naga who has thus departed with contempt.
Having encountered him, you would know Puṇṇa to be of fierce splendor;
I think of him as if he were a heap of ashes.
"He will surely do it quickly.
"There might be poison for one who eats stones,
for a water-snake that feeds on stones;"
“Even for a red-headed serpent, no poison exists.
“This has been heard from the Arahants:”
For those who are self-restrained and ascetic;
having given gifts here,
the donors go to heaven.
While living, give gifts,
if you have anything to give;
this Naga is of great psychic power.
He is full of splendor and difficult to overcome;
with that, I shall sting you,
and he will reduce you to ashes.”
“I have heard this, good sir,
from self-restrained ascetics: that by giving gifts here in this world, [one gains great merit].”
The donors go to heaven;
you yourself give while you are still living,
if there is anything for you to give.
This one is named Ajamukhī,
full of fierce splendor;
with her I shall bite you.
She will reduce him to ashes—
she who is the daughter of Dhatarattha, my half-sister.
She, with the face of a stinging insect,
was full of fierce heat; had I poured her down upon the ground,
[it would have been disastrous].
O Brahmadatta, understand this:
the grasses, creepers, and medicinal herbs would surely wither away without a doubt.
If I were to cause it to fall from above,
O Brahmadatta, know this:
for seven years the rain would not fall.
Neither rain nor snow shall fall.
If I were to pour it out upon the water,
O Brahmadatta, know this for certain.
“As many water-born creatures as there may be—
fish and turtles— that might die when the world-drenching rain falls.”
Established at Prayāga,
having swallowed the *koma*,
he plunged into the river Yamunā.
“When the illustrious lord of the world had cleared Bārāṇasī on all sides, I,
the son of that bull among serpents, [entered it].”
“O Brahmin, they know me as Subhoga.
“If indeed I were the son of the bull among serpents,
the King of Kāsi, the lord of the immortals;”
One of your fathers was of great power,
but among mortals your mother was peerless;
such a one as she does not deserve a brahmin [as her husband].
“Even to give away his life, he is of great power.
“Leaning against a tree,
you shot at a deer that had come to drink;”
Thus pierced, he fled far away with the speed of an arrow,
moving swiftly; you saw him fallen.
In the great forest of the wilderness,
having taken a deer carcass,
he came to the banyan tree in the evening.
Resounding with the cries of parrots and mynas,
variegated and carpeted with grass,
it was delightful, echoing with the songs of cuckoos.
It was surely green with young grass.
There he appeared to you,
radiant with supernatural power and glory.
My brother is of great power,
surrounded by maidens;
you have been attended upon by him.
Though you were satisfied with all desires,
you have betrayed one who was free from malice;
thus has this enmity come upon you here.
Quickly stretch out your neck;
I will not give you your life.
Let your enmity reach its brother's side.
“I shall cut off your head.
“The reciter, the one devoted to begging,
the Brahmin who maintains the sacrificial fire;”
On these three grounds,
a brahmin is beyond reproach.
As for that which was filled by Dhatarattha—
Having plunged into the Yamunā River,
he shines forth, all-golden,
reaching up to the mountain of Yama.
There, those tigers among men,
my uterine brothers,
will speak to you as they see fit.
"So shall it be for you, O Brahmin.
Sacrifices, the Vedas, and great wealth in this world are impermanent, associated with what is transient."
For one who reviles that which is most excellent abandons both wealth and the Dhamma of the virtuous.
Noble lords of the earth [abandon] their learning and the earth itself.
The Vessas [attained] through agriculture and service, and the Suddas;
they each approached according to their respective stations,
for it is said that these were established by the Vasins.
Dhātā, Vidhātā, Varuṇa, Kuvera,
Soma, Yama, Candima, Vāyu, and Sūriya— even these,
having offered sacrifice in various ways, [did not escape death].
To those who recite the Vedas and likewise to all their desires—
[he gave] five hundred expanded bows.
He was Ajuna, powerful and like Bhimasena.
Sahassabāhu, peerless on earth,
he too then kindled the sacrificial fire;
he who for a long time fed the brahmins.
With food and drink according to his means,
with a confident heart and full of appreciation,
he became a certain god of great wealth.
He who was able to feed the sacrificial fire with ghee— its seat vast and its color like that of a celestial being—
having performed that sacrifice according to the excellent ritual manual, [attained the highest state].
He attained the divine state of Mucalinda.
Of great majesty, living for a thousand years,
he who went forth was beautiful to behold and sublime.
Having abandoned his boundless kingdom along with his army,
King Duddīpa went to heaven,
he who had conquered the ocean reaching to its very shore.
Having offered a magnificent, beautiful sacrificial post made of gold,
that Vessānara was reborn as a certain god of great wealth.
By whose power the beautiful Ganges flows,
carrying curds as thick as the ocean,
he served the fire with his feet covered in straw and sought [the goal].
Aṅga went to the city of Sahassakkha.
Of great psychic power, illustrious,
and a preeminent god, he was the general of Vāsava in the triple heaven.
Thus, having destroyed his impurity through the Soma sacrifice,
Subhoga became a certain deity.
He caused this world and the next to be made [for him].
The powerful, illustrious, and excellent deity also then set ablaze the Bhāgīrathī,
the Himavat, and the vulture.
Mālāgiri, Himavā, and Gijjhakūṭa,
Sudassana, Nisabha, and Kuvera;
these and other great mountains—
They say that sacrifices were performed by the city-dwellers;
they say that one who is a reciter, endowed with the qualities of mantras,
and devoted to austerity is fit for the offering.
The water splashing on the shore of the ocean is swallowed by the sea; it is not to be drunk.
The sacrificial sites are many upon the earth.
"Brahmins exist for Vāsava; appearing in the eastern,
western, southern, and northern directions,
they produce the Veda."
“Indeed, for the wise, the Kali age is no hardship,
nor is it a misfortune for those who have mastered the Vedas,
because they do not perceive the world as having the nature of a mirage.”
The qualities of illusion do not outweigh wisdom.
The Vedas provide no refuge for that man who betrays his friends and destroys living beings.
The fire does not protect one who has been served;
it consumes the mortal who is full of faults and performs ignoble deeds.
And all mortals, together with their wealth and possessions—
A fire kindled with wood mixed with grass,
burning, is not satisfied even by an inexhaustible supply of fuel;
who would consider such a fire to be well-fed?
Just as milk, being subject to transformation,
becomes curd and then even butter;
so too, fire is subject to transformation.
The fire-element descends into him who is engaged in yoga.
Once it has entered the flame, it is no longer seen,
whether in dry wood or even in fresh wood.
Fire does not arise without the friction of the fire-sticks, nor is it produced without effort.
For if fire were to abide within itself, it would never cease.
Even if all the forests in the world were to dry up— both the dry wood and the fresh—
and the dry wood were to burst into flame;
If a man performs merit by means of wood and grass,
he becomes a consumer of food, possessing a smoky crest and great radiance;
likewise, charcoal-burners, salt-makers, and cooks [attain such states].
They might even perform the merit of cremating the body. But if they do not perform this merit here,
having instead warmed themselves at the sacrificial fire through Vedic recitation;
No one in the world performs merit,
[thinking] "A man who eats shall become smoke-crested and majestic.
For how could one who is honored by the world [act thus]?
The foul-smelling scent that is disliked by many,
which mortals avoid— that very thing,
though it be unpraiseworthy, one who perceives its dual nature should eat.
Some among the gods say, "We are Śikhins," while others say,
"We are Mlecchas"; all of these speak what is false.
Neither fire nor water is a deity;
one should understand Vessānara as the performer of karma, a body without consciousness and not bound by sense faculties.
How could one who commits evil deeds ever travel the path to a happy rebirth?
He who seeks a livelihood here, having overcome all things— such a person is called a conqueror.
"Brahmā is an attendant of the Chief One;
he possesses all power and is self-mastering.
For what purpose would he, being uncreated himself, pay homage to one who is created?"
In the past, for the sake of honor, they scattered forth false words that were unbearable to contemplate with hatred;
yet when those gains and honors did not manifest, [they fell away].
Living beings have established their respective duties: the noble ones (ariyas) the study of the Vedas,
the lords of men (janindas) the tilling of the earth,
the merchants (vessas) agriculture, and the laborers (suddas) service.
They have each arrived at their respective places;
they say, "These ones have attained mastery.
And may these words be true.
Just as it has been said by the brahmins:
"One who is not a khattiya can never obtain kingship,
nor can one who is not a brahmin study the words of the mantras."
"A Vessa would not perform ploughing,
nor would a Sudda be released from the service of others"—
since this statement is untrue, [it is rejected].
Those with bloated bellies speak lies;
those of little wisdom place their faith in them,
but the wise see that for themselves alone.
For the Khattiyas pay tribute to the Vessas,
and the Brāhmaṇas wander about taking up their weapons;
such a world, thus agitated and shattered—
Why does Brahmā not make the world upright?
For if he were the Lord of the entire world,
Brahmā, the master of many beings and the progenitor of all creatures;
Why did he burn the entire world with misfortune?
Why did he make the entire world unhappy?
For if he were indeed the Lord of the entire world...
Why did Brahmā, the lord of many beings and of progeny,
act unrighteously toward the world through illusion, falsehood, and the intoxication of pride?
For if that Brahmā were the Lord of all the world, the master of many beings and the ruler of creatures,
he would be unrighteous, O Ariṭṭha.
When the Dhamma exists, one who discerns what is contrary to the Dhamma—
having destroyed worms, moths, snakes,
frogs, maggots, and flies— is purified.
These things are unworthy and contrary to the many teachings of the Kambujas;
for if he who kills were thereby purified, [then...]
Even if he has killed, such a person goes to a heavenly state;
for they would kill one who addresses others as "friend," as well as those who place their trust in them.
Neither deer, nor cattle,
nor even oxen ever pray for their own destruction; yet here,
those seeking a livelihood struggle and strive.
At sacrifices, the foolish slaughter living beings as animals;
at the erection of sacrificial posts and animal-binding rites,
they lead the victim’s face about with colorful cloths.
This sacrificial post of yours shall be a cow of plenty for the sake of the beyond;
it will be eternal in the life to come.
And if, upon the post, there be gems, conch shells, and pearls—
Grain, wealth, silver, and gold;
even if one were to milk all the desires from the three heavens using dry wood or fresh wood as the milking vessel—
Let many communities possessing the threefold knowledge perform sacrifices;
let them not cause anyone who is not a brahmin to sacrifice.
And from where [could there be] a sacrificial post adorned with gems, conch shells, and pearls?
Grain, wealth, silver, and gold—
even from dry wood or even from fresh [trees],
how could one milk all the desires of the Thirty-three Gods?
Deceitful, cruel, and deluded fools lead one astray with words and smiles;
"Take this fire and give me my wealth."
Then you will be happy in all desires.
Having entered that sacrificial fire as a refuge,
they lead you away by means of their minds and their splendors.
Having shaved off their hair and beard and trimmed their nails,
they squander the wealth of the Videhans like crows seizing an owl in secret.
Though they are but one, many gather together;
having eaten various foods and practiced deception,
these deceivers shave their heads and set out upon the path of sacrifice.
For thus was he deceived by the brahmins;
though he was alone, they approached him in great numbers.
Plundering him through their various stratagems, they overwhelmed him.
They carry off the wealth of one who has been seen by means of one who has not been seen.
Even when commanded by kings,
they take that wealth of his and carry it away.
Such as they are, those non-existent ones who are like thieves,
Ariṭṭha, are not executed in this world.
"You are the right arm of Indra," [they say].
At sacrifices they cut off the splinter-bone;
even if that were true, Maghava would have his arm cut off—
how then could Indra, the Lord, conquer the Asuras?
If Maghavan were to possess that very emptiness,
he would indeed be an inviolable slayer, a supreme god;
these Brahmins are but empty-minded conjurors.
This deception is visible right here in the world:
Mālāgiri, Himavā, Gijjha,
Sudassana, Nisabha, and Kuvera.
These and other great mountains were built as cities by those who perform sacrifices;
for they are made of bricks according to their respective forms.
The city built by those who perform sacrifices does not provide such assistance as mountains do—
other directions that remain immovable with their standing rocks.
There are no bricks or stones there for a long time,
nor is iron or copper produced there;
yet they continue to praise this sacrifice.
The city-dwellers, performing sacrifices, said:
"Let there not be [one who is] a reciter endowed with the merit of mantras,
an ascetic devoted to the practice of begging."
The water splashing on the shore of the ocean is swallowed by the sea;
it is not to be drunk even by one who knows all the Vedas,
even if there are more than a thousand such as him.
Rivers flow even when they have fallen into filth;
yet their waters do not thereby become corrupted in taste—
why then is the incomparable ocean undrinkable?
Whatever wells there are here in this world of living beings that have been dug by those who dig wells with salt water—
none of them are fit for the consumption of a brahmin.
"Water is not for drinking; let them not perceive two flavors.
Who was the wife of whom in the ancient past?
Mind produced human beings in the beginning."
By that Dhamma no one is inferior;
thus they speak of the analysis of relinquishment.
Even a son of a caṇḍāla, having mastered the Vedas by chance...
A wise and skillful person may recite these mantras;
yet his head shall not split into seven pieces,
for these mantras were made for one's own destruction.
Speech that is harsh, greedy, and grasping,
difficult to relinquish and fallen into the path of poetry—
the mind of fools is settled upon what is uneven.
Those of little wisdom place their faith in this:
that in the strength of a lion, a tiger, or a leopard, there is no human power to be found.
The human state is to be regarded as like that of cattle,
for their births are both unequal and yet equal.
And even if a king, having conquered the earth...
One who is long-lived and has obedient followers will himself conquer the host of enemies,
and his offspring shall always be happy.
The Kshatriya mantras and the three Vedas—
these are equal in meaning; yet without having determined their true meaning, [one does not understand them].
One does not perceive it, as if a path were covered by a flood.
The Kṣatriya mantras and the three Vedas—
these are equal in their meaning.
Gain and loss, disrepute and fame—
all these four things are common to them all;
just as even outcasts, for the sake of wealth and grain, [strive].
In the past, many performed deeds upon this earth;
and even today, communities possessing the threefold knowledge likewise perform many deeds upon this earth.
Those who are equal to slaves,
ever eager and intent upon the strands of sensual pleasure,
perform various works throughout the earth.
“Then those of little wisdom will be twice as lustful.
“To whom do the kettledrums, tabors,
conchs, drums, and cymbals belong?”
Proceeding ahead,
making the bull among charioteers smile,
whose [face] with a golden band—
With a variegated, lightning-colored [garment],
young, and girt with a quiver—
who is this coming, radiant with glory?
Like a flame struck from a flint,
resembling glowing acacia embers,
her face shines with radiant beauty.
Who comes with splendor and radiance?
To whom belongs the beautiful golden parasol, complete with its ribs?
Who comes with the splendor of the sun’s rays?
Whose body, having been embraced, [is thus adorned]?
The supreme yak-tail whisk was held one above the other over the head of that person of excellent merit.
Whose are these fans with handles of gold and jewels, variegated and soft?
They move about with their mouths open on both sides,
possessing the hue of acacia charcoal,
scorched as if by the mouth of a furnace.
The earrings, beautiful and curved,
shine on both sides of the face.
Whose [face] is touched by the wind?
Polished, soft, and dark,
they beautify the forehead like lightning flashing across the sky.
To whom do these eyes belong,
so long and broad?
Who shines with such large eyes?
Whose is this woolly face?
Whose are these lips,
pure like the form of a conch shell?
The teeth of one who speaks shine like jasmine buds;
whose [teeth] are like lac-juice?
With hands and feet well-groomed,
who is this one endowed with lips like the *bimba* fruit,
who shines by day like the sun?
In the Himalayas,
like a great sal tree in full bloom—
who is this one clad in white robes?
The victory-banner shines like the moon,
strewn with golden knobs and variegated with jeweled shafts.
Who is it that, having entered the assembly,
draws his sword with its jeweled hilt,
adorned with gold?
The stitching of the mind has been well-done;
who is it that now unfastens the feet,
having paid homage to the Great Seer?
For those Dhataraṭṭha nāgas,
possessed of psychic power and renown,
were born of Samuddajā.
"These nāgas possess great supernormal power.
Thus ends the sixth Jātaka, the Bhūridatta-jātaka.
